name: World Schools Debate
summary: Teams of three debate prepared and surprise motions in long speeches, with points of information, judged on style, content and strategy.
who: High school students in teams of three to five (three speak in each round). It is the format of the World Schools Debating Championships, and the NSDA offers it at its national tournament and many local ones.
resolution: "Motions" (This House would..., This House believes...). Some are prepared ahead; others are impromptu and announced shortly before the round.

speeches.name: First Proposition
speeches.speaker: P1
speeches.job: Define the motion, set out the proposition's case and its first arguments.

speeches.name: First Opposition
speeches.speaker: O1
speeches.job: Respond to the definition and case, and set out the opposition's case.

speeches.name: Second Proposition
speeches.speaker: P2
speeches.job: Rebuild, rebut, and add the proposition's remaining arguments.

speeches.name: Second Opposition
speeches.speaker: O2
speeches.job: Rebuild, rebut, and add the opposition's remaining arguments.

speeches.name: Third Proposition
speeches.speaker: P3
speeches.job: Mostly rebuttal: organize the clash and answer the opposition.

speeches.name: Third Opposition
speeches.speaker: O3
speeches.job: Mostly rebuttal: organize the clash and answer the proposition.

speeches.name: Opposition Reply
speeches.speaker: O1 or O2
speeches.job: A short, fair overview of the debate from the opposition's view. Given by the first or second speaker.

speeches.name: Proposition Reply
speeches.speaker: P1 or P2
speeches.job: A short, fair overview of the debate from the proposition's view. The last speech of the round.

prep.note: No prep time between speeches. For impromptu motions, teams get one hour from the motion's release to the start of the round (USA World Schools Debate Invitational rules), with only a dictionary and a one-volume encyclopedia or almanac.

poi.note: Points of information may be offered only by the other team, only during the six eight-minute speeches, and not in the first or last minute. The speaker may accept or decline. Reply speeches have no points of information.

rewards: Style, content and strategy, weighted 40%, 40% and 20% on the ballot
Arguments about principle and real-world examples, not quoted evidence cards
Taking and answering points of information well
start: Practice an eight-minute speech built from two arguments, each with an example.
Practice impromptu prep: one hour, a team of three, paper only.
Offer and answer points of information in practice: one short sentence, then sit down.
Learn the reply speech: it summarizes the debate's main clashes; it is not a fourth constructive.
varies: Prep for impromptu motions: one hour at the USA World Schools Debate Invitational and the World Schools Championships; local tournaments sometimes use less.
Materials: international and NSDA invitational rules forbid electronic devices in rounds except a phone used only as a timer; local tournaments may differ.
The mix of prepared and impromptu motions differs by tournament.

p: Speeches alternate between the proposition and the opposition, three per side, then each side gives one reply speech, the opposition first. While the other team speaks, debaters may stand and offer a **point of information**, a short question or statement the speaker can accept or decline.
World Schools favors arguments of principle and well-chosen examples over stacks of quoted evidence, and it rewards a team that works together across all three speakers.
